title: Impact of aging on the pharmacokinetic profile of everolimus in male mice

sections.abstract:
Age-related changes in drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters can alter pharmacokinetics, yet data on everolimus, a widely used mTOR inhibitor, remain limited. This study investigated the pharmacokinetic profile of everolimus in male C57BL/6J mice at three life stages—young (≈ 9 weeks), adult (≈ 23 weeks), and old (≈ 56 weeks)—and examined whether age-related changes in hepatic and intestinal Cyp3a11 and Abcb1a/b (P-gp; P-glycoprotein) expression parallel these alterations. Mice received a single oral dose of everolimus (5 mg/kg, ZT1), and plasma and hepatic concentrations were quantified over 24 h by validated HPLC-UV, with non-compartmental analysis performed ( n = 5 per age group per time point). In drug-naïve, age-matched cohorts, gene and protein expression were measured by qPCR and western blot ( n = 5 per age group).

The area under the concentration–time curve (AUC total ) was 129% greater in young mice and 86% more in mature mice compared to old mice (young vs. old, p < 0.05). Peak plasma concentration (C max ) also decreased with age (young + 95%, adult + 72% compared to elderly; p < 0.01 and p < 0.05). Oral clearance (CL/F) increased by 68% in adults and 230% in older individuals compared to young animals, whereas the apparent volume of distribution (Vd/F) climbed by 47% and 187%, respectively. In liver, Abcb1a remained unchanged across age groups, whereas Abcb1b transcripts rose ~ 1.5-fold in old vs. young mice ( p < 0.001). Hepatic Cyp3a11 declined stepwise, falling by ~ 55% in old animals ( p < 0.01). At the protein level, total hepatic P-gp dropped in adult and old mice (− 45% vs. young, p < 0.05) and Cyp3a protein showed a non-significant downward trend. In ileum, Abcb1a increased sharply with age (adult ≈ 5-fold, old ≈ 7-fold vs. young), translating to a ~ 5-fold rise in P-gp protein in adult mice ( p < 0.01); Abcb1b transcripts were unchanged. Ileal Cyp3a11 mRNA peaked in adults (≈ 3-fold vs. young, p < 0.05), although Cyp3a protein differences did not reach significance.

These findings suggest that reduced everolimus bioavailability in older mice is primarily driven by increased intestinal P-gp–mediated efflux rather than hepatic metabolism, supporting the need for age-adjusted dosing to optimize therapeutic outcomes across the lifespan.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s40360-025-01079-8.

Keywords: Age, Everolimus, Cyp3a, P-glycoprotein, C57BL/6J mice
sections.introduction:
In mammals, various anatomical, physiological and biochemical changes occur throughout the lifespan, and age is an important factor causing inter-individual variability in drug treatment [ 1 ]. Age-related physiological changes may lead to alterations in drug pharmacokinetics. Accordingly, the efficacy and toxicity of drugs can show variations depending on the age [ 2 ]. Since pediatric and elderly populations show increased or decreased sensitivity to some chemicals compared to adults, optimization of dosage may be required based on the age [ 3 , 4 ].

Age-dependent changes occur in the processes of absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination [ 1 , 3 , 5 ]. Factors related to absorption such as gastric pH, gastric emptying time, intestinal transit time, secretion of bile and pancreatic enzymes, show differences between pediatric population and adults [ 1 ]. In a study in rats at different ages [ 6 ], changes were shown to occur in the microvascular structure of jejunal villi and endothelial structure of villous capillaries. Moreover, microvascular permeability of the aged rats was found to be two times higher than adults [ 6 ]. In the intestine, levels of drug metabolizing enzymes such as cytochrome (CYP) 3A4, CYP3A5 and efflux protein P-gp may also change with age and affect bioavailability for orally administered drugs [ 7 ].

Age-related changes in hepatic CYP450 enzyme expression/activity greatly affect drug metabolism [ 8 – 12 ]. Expression levels of many Cyp3a enzymes in the older rats showed marked decrease indicating a reduction in metabolic capacity [ 13 ]. It is shown that increasing age caused severe impairment of Cyp2d and Cyp3a metabolism in the geriatric (18-month‐old) rat liver fractions [ 14 ]. In some studies with tacrolimus, pediatric transplant recipients required 2-to 4- fold higher doses than adults to achieve the same plasma levels and such differences were attributed to the different Cyp3a levels [ 10 ].

Distribution phase related factors such as membrane permeability, plasma protein binding, and body composition may also change depending on age and affect drug pharmacokinetics [ 15 – 17 ]. Plasma protein levels vary significantly during aging and it was shown that plasma albumin levels decreased from 8 to 19 months of age in mice [ 18 ]. The body fat mass in mice showed a regular increase with age between 8 and 56 weeks [ 19 ]. This may cause an increase with age in the volume of distribution of lipophilic molecules such as everolimus. Anatomical structure of the kidney, glomerular filtration, tubular secretion, tubular reabsorption functions and renal blood flow are some of the age-related factors affecting drug excretion [ 15 – 17 ]. Due to these changes, there are age-related decreases in the clearance of many drugs that are primarily eliminated by the kidneys. These decreases may lead to higher plasma drug levels [ 15 ].

Everolimus is an oral immunosuppressive drug, used both to prevent organ transplant rejection and in the treatment of cancer [ 20 ]. Everolimus inhibits mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) serine/threonine kinase signal transduction pathway which regulates cell growth, proliferation and survival [ 21 ].

In this study, we investigated the age-dependent pharmacokinetics of everolimus in C57BL/6J male mice of three different age groups: young (~ 9 weeks old), adult (~ 23 weeks old), and old (~ 56 weeks old). We also evaluated Cyp3a and Abcb1a/b mRNA and CYP3A and P-gp protein expressions in liver and intestinal tissues of animals and determined their relationship with the pharmacokinetic data. To our knowledge, this is the first study examining the age-dependent pharmacokinetics of everolimus and showing age-related changes in the hepatic and intestinal Cyp3a and Abcb1a/b mRNA and protein expressions of mice.
sections.methods:
C57BL/6J male mice (20–24 g) were supplied from Istanbul University Aziz Sancar Institute of Experimental Medicine Laboratory Animals Unit. Age groups were defined according to established physiological aging frameworks for C57BL/6J mice [ 22 ], classifying 8–9 weeks as young, 22–23 weeks as adult, and 54–58 weeks as old (middle-aged). The experiments were performed in Istanbul University Faculty of Pharmacy Experimental Animal Unit (EDEHAB) under standardized conditions. Mice were housed in polystyrene cages up to five animals in the room equipped with temperature (22 ± 1 °C) and humidity (55 ± 10%) control. Mice were kept with 12 h of light (L) in alternation with 12 h of darkness (D) (LD 12:12). Everolimus administration was carried out at ZT1 (i.e. 1 h after light onset). No restriction applied to the animals and water/food were provided ad libitum throughout the experiments. The ethical approval was obtained from the local ethics committee of experimental animals of Istanbul University (IUHADYEK, no: 2017/ 295816).

Everolimus was purchased from ApexBio Technology (TX, USA). All other chemicals and solvents were purchased from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany).

For pharmacokinetic analyses, everolimus was dissolved in propylene glycol: distilled water (50:50, v/v) and administered to the mice (5 mg/kg; per oral) as a single dose at ZT1. Blood samples were collected under 1% isoflurane anesthesia by cardiac puncture at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 12 and 24 h after everolimus administration ( n = 5 for each time point). All blood samples were collected in EDTA tubes (BD Vacutainer ® , NJ, USA) and the tubes were centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min (Hettich, Germany) to obtain plasma. Liver samples were weighed and homogenized with a mechanical homogenizer (Art-Miccra-D1, Germany) in 1:1 (w/w) in PBS. Everolimus plasma levels were determined by validated High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC).

For mRNA and protein expression studies, young, adult and old male healthy control mice ( n = 5) were included in the study. Liver and ileum samples were collected. Feces immediately removed from the ileum samples, the ileum was opened, and the mucosa was collected into a clean tube with a scalpel. All tissue samples were immediately immersed in liquid nitrogen and frozen, then stored at -80 °C until analyses.

Everolimus concentrations in mouse plasma and liver were determined using the method described by Ozturk Civelek et al. [ 23 ]. HPLC system consisting of 2695 separations module and 2489 UV/Vis detector (Waters, USA). C8 reversed phase column (150 × 4.6 mm, 5 μm; Phenomenex, USA) with a C8 guard column (4 × 3.0 mm; Phenomenex, USA) employed for the separation. The mobile phase consisted of acetonitrile-ammonium acetate 0,01 M (60:40, v/v, pH: 4) and the flow rate was 1 mL/min. Column temperature was set to 50 °C. Repaglinide (Biocon Limited, India) is used as an internal standard (IS). Everolimus and IS were detected at 278 nm. In the extraction step, proteins were precipitated with methanol and 0,25 M zinc sulphate, then, everolimus was separated by solid-phase extraction (SPE). Firstly, Oasis HLB 1 cc/30 mg cartridge (Waters, USA) was washed with 1 ml of methanol and then pre-conditioned with 1 ml of HPLC-grade water. After applying 200 µl of plasma or liver homogenate and IS on the cartridge, the cartridges were washed with 250 µl water-methanol (95:5; v/v) and everolimus was eluted from the column with 250 µl methanol. Method validation was made according to ICH Guidelines (10.5167/uzh-104384). Linearity, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, detection limit (LOD), and quantification limit (LOQ) were calculated [ 23 ].

The pharmacokinetic parameters of everolimus were obtained using the non-compartmental analysis method. Everolimus peak plasma concentrations (C max ) and time to reach peak concentration (t max ) values were obtained directly from the plasma concentration-time curves. The area under the plasma concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC 0–24 h ) was calculated by using the linear trapezoidal rule. The total area under the plasma concentration-time curve from time zero to infinity (AUC total ) was calculated as the sum of AUC 0–24 h and extrapolated part after the last sampling time using the standard formula (Concentration at 24 h (C 24h ) / Elimination rate constant (k el ) was obtained by plotting the exponential graph using the last four time points. Elimination half-life (t 1/2 ) was calculated by the Eq. 0.693/k el . The apparent oral clearance (CL/F) after the peroral dose was calculated by using the equation Dose/AUC total , and the apparent volume of distribution (Vd/F) was calculated by the formula (CL/F)/k el .

Liver and mucosal ileum samples were homogenized with ceramic beads in RIPA lysis buffer (Santa Cruz, USA) with Bead Ruptor 12 (Omni International, USA). Protein concentrations were determined using Qubit Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Scientific, USA) and Qubit 2.0 fluorometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). Proteins were separated on 4–10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred to 0.45 μm PVDF membrane (Millipore, USA) by using Mini Trans-Blot cell (Bio-Rad, USA) for 2 h at 120 V. After blocking in 5% non-fat milk, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies against P-gp (A11747, Abclonal) and CYP3A (A13484, Abclonal) overnight at 4 °C, or with GAPDH (AC002, Abclonal) for 1 h at room temperature (RT). Membranes were probed with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at 1 h RT. Chemiluminescence was detected using Clarity Max Western ECL Substrate (Bio-Rad, USA). The density of the bands was quantified using Image Lab 6.0 (Bio-Rad, USA) and calculated relative to GAPDH.

Total RNA from liver and mucosal ileum samples was homogenized with ceramic beads in lysis buffer of Echotech Total RNA Kit (E2075, EcoTech Biotechnology, TR) and purification performed as manufacturer’s directions. cDNA was synthesized from Total RNA using High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems, USA). The real-time PCR was performed using SensiFAST™ SYBR ® No-ROX Kit (Biolinei USA) with Bio-Rad CFX96 (USA). Relative mRNA abundance was calculated using the 2-ΔΔ Ct method [ 24 ], 36b4 used as reference control. The following primers were used:

Abcb1a : AAT GTT TCG TTA TGC AGG TTG GC (Forward; F) and TGG CTC TTT TAT CGG CCT CAC (Reverese; R); Abcb1b : GAG ACA GGA TAT AAG CTG GTT CG (F) and CGC CCC TTT AAC ACT AGA AGC A (R); Cyp3a11 :GAC AAA CAA GCA GGG ATG GAC (F) and CCA AGC TGA TTG CTA GGA GCA (R); Gapdh : AGG TCG GTG TGA ACG GAT TTG (F) and TGT AGA CCA TGT AGT TGA GGT CA (R).

Data were presented as mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA were performed to evaluate the difference between groups. The differences between any two groups were evaluated with post-hoc Tukey test. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test and homogeneity of variances using the Brown–Forsythe test for all datasets subjected to one-way ANOVA. All statistical analysis was performed, and all figures were created with Graphpad Prism version 9.0.0 for Windows, GraphPad Software, San Diego (CA, USA).
sections.results:
After a single 5 mg kg⁻¹ oral dose of everolimus, plasma pharmacokinetic parameters for young (8–9 wk), adult (22–23 wk) and old (54–58 wk) male mice are summarized in Fig. 1 ; Table 1 . Time to reach the maximum concentration (t max ) was essentially identical across ages (≈ 0.7–0.8 h). Peak plasma concentration (C max ) declined progressively: young > adult > old. Values in young mice (4.02 ± 0.30 µg mL⁻¹) were significantly higher than in old mice ( p < 0.05) and adults also exceeded olds ( p < 0.05). Correspondingly, systemic exposure (AUC 0–24 h and AUC total ) was ~ 2-fold greater in young versus old animals ( p < 0.05). Differences between young and adult, and between adult and old, did not reach significance. Apparent oral clearance (CL/F) rose from 2.26 ± 0.40 mL h⁻¹ in young mice to 7.38 ± 1.79 mL h⁻¹ in old mice ( p < 0.05). Apparent volume of distribution (Vd/F) more than doubled in old animals (52.91 ± 5.86 mL) compared with young (20.02 ± 3.08 mL, p < 0.001) and was also higher than in adults ( p < 0.01). The terminal half-life (t 1/2 ) remained stable (≈ 5–6 h) across groups, suggesting that age-related increases in CL/F were offset by parallel rises in Vd/F. Collectively, these data indicate that advancing age in C57BL/6J mice is accompanied by reduced everolimus bioavailability and increased apparent clearance and distribution, leading to markedly lower systemic exposure in old animals.

Plasma concentration–time profile and AUC 0–24 h of everolimus in young, adult, and old mice. ( A ) Plasma concentration–time curves following a single oral dose of everolimus (5 mg/kg) in young, adult, and old male C57BL/6J mice. Data are expressed as mean ± SD ( n = 5 per group). ( B ) Area under the plasma concentration–time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC 0–24 h ) for each age group. * p < 0.05 vs. indicated groups (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc test)

Plasma Pharmacokinetic parameters for young, adult, and old mice after administration of per oral everolimus 5 mg/kg

t max : The time when the maximum concentration is reached. C max : The maximum concentration. t 1/2 : Elimination half-life. AUC 0-24 h : Area under the curve between 0 to 24 h. AUC total : Area under the total curve. CL/F: Clearance. Vd/F: Volume of distribution. Values are given as mean ± SD (standard error or mean). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01 young vs. old; # p < 0.05, ## p < 0.01 adult vs. old

Figure 2 A illustrates the liver concentration–time profiles, and Fig. 2 B depicts the corresponding AUC 0–24 h values for young, adult and old mice. Key pharmacokinetic indices are summarized in Table 2 . C max and AUC 0–24 h both fall sharply from the young to the adult group and then rebound in the old group, producing a U-shaped profile. Relative to the young group, the adult mice exhibited an ~ 80% reduction in hepatic C max (23.7 ± 5.12 vs. 4.87 ± 1.02 µg/mL; p < 0.05) and an ~ 57% decrease in AUC 0–24 h (121.2 ± 32.8 vs. 52.5 ± 19.5 µg.h/mL). In contrast, comparison of the adult and old cohorts revealed a greater than three-fold rise in both parameters, with AUC 0–24 h reaching 235.6 ± 60.2 µg.h/mL in the old mice ( p < 0.05). t max remained consistent across ages (≈ 0.7–1 h), indicating that the age effect reflects differences in magnitude rather than rate of liver uptake.

Liver concentration–time profile and AUC 0–24 h of everolimus in young, adult, and old mice. ( A ) Liver concentration–time curves following a single oral dose of everolimus (5 mg/kg) in young, adult, and old male C57BL/6J mice. Data are expressed as mean ± SD ( n = 5 per group). ( B ) Area under the plasma concentration–time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC 0–24 h ) for each age group. * p < 0.05 vs. indicated groups (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc test)

Liver Pharmacokinetic parameters for young, adult, and old mice after dosing of per oral 5 mg/kg everolimus

t max : The time when the maximum concentration is reached. C max : The maximum concentration. AUC 0-24 h : Area under the curve between 0 to 24 h. Values are given as mean ± SD (standard error or mean). # p < 0.05 adult vs. old; + p < 0.05, ++ p < 0.01 young vs. adult

As shown in Fig. 3 , age exerted isoform-specific and post-transcriptional effects on the Abcb1 /P-gp system. Abcb1a remained unchanged across the three age groups (Fig. 3 A), whereas Abcb1b transcripts rose significantly with age, reaching ~ 1.8-fold higher levels in old mice than in both young and adult cohorts ( p < 0.001, Fig. 3 B). In contrast, total P-gp protein abundance fell by ~ 25–30% in both adult and old animals relative to young controls ( p < 0.05; Fig. 3 C), with no difference between the two older groups. Representative immunoblots are provided in Fig. 3 D. These data indicate that, despite an age-related up-regulation of Abcb1b transcription, hepatic P-gp protein is down-regulated from early adulthood onward, pointing to post-transcriptional control mechanisms.

Age-dependent changes in hepatic P-glycoprotein (P-gp) expression in young, adult, and old mice. ( A ) Relative Abcb1a mRNA expression normalized to Gapdh. ( B ) Relative Abcb1b mRNA expression normalized to Gapdh. ( C ) Quantification of P-gp protein levels normalized to GAPDH. ( D ) Representative Western blot images of P-gp and GAPDH protein levels. Data are presented as mean ± SD; * p < 0.05, *** p < 0.001 vs. indicated groups ( n = 5 per group)

Figure 4 illustrates age-related changes in the principal murine Cyp3a isoform. Liver Cyp3a11 mRNA declined progressively with age, falling by ∼45% in adult mice ( p < 0.01) and by ∼65% in old mice ( p < 0.001) relative to the young group (Fig. 4 A). In contrast, CYP3A protein abundance showed only a modest downward trend and did not differ significantly between age groups (Fig. 4 B), as confirmed by the representative immunoblots (Fig. 4 C). These data indicate that ageing reduces CYP3A transcription in liver, whereas steady-state protein levels remain comparatively stable, suggesting post-transcriptional buffering of CYP3A expression.

Age-dependent changes in hepatic Cyp3a expression and protein levels in young, adult, and old mice. ( A ) Hepatic Cyp3a mRNA expression normalized to Gapdh. ( B ) CYP3A protein levels normalized to GAPDH. ( C ) Representative Western blot images showing CYP3A and GAPDH protein expression in liver samples from each age group. Data are presented as mean ± SD; ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001 vs. indicated groups ( n = 5 per group)

In the ileum, age affected P-gp primarily at the protein level (Fig. 5 ). Abcb1a transcripts showed a gradual, non-significant rise from young to old mice, whereas Abcb1b mRNA remained essentially constant across groups (Fig. 5 A, B). By contrast, total P-gp protein increased markedly in adulthood: adult animals displayed a ~ 4-fold higher P-gp/GAPDH ratio than young controls ( p < 0.01), while values in the old group were intermediate and did not differ significantly from either of the other cohorts (Fig. 5 C). Representative immunoblots are presented in Fig. 5 D. These findings indicate that ageing up-regulates P-gp in the intestinal mucosa mainly through post-transcriptional mechanisms, with the greatest elevation occurring at mid-life.

Age-dependent changes in ileal P-glycoprotein (P-gp) expression in young, adult, and old mice. ( A ) Relative Abcb1a mRNA expression normalized to Gapdh. ( B ) Relative Abcb1b mRNA expression normalized to Gapdh. ( C ) Quantification of P-gp protein levels normalized to GAPDH. ( D ) Representative Western blot images of P-gp and GAPDH protein levels. Data are presented as mean ± SD; ** p < 0.01 vs. indicated groups ( n = 5 per group)

As depicted in Fig. 6 , neither the transcript nor the protein levels of Cyp3a exhibited a statistically significant age dependence. Cyp3a11 mRNA showed a modest, non-significant increase in adult mice relative to young, with values in the old group returning toward baseline (Fig. 6 A). Total CYP3A protein abundance remained virtually unchanged across the three cohorts, despite considerable inter-individual variability (Fig. 6 B, representative blots in Fig. 6 C). Taken together, these findings indicate that intestinal CYP3A expression is largely stable over lifespan and is unlikely to account for the pronounced age-related differences observed in everolimus pharmacokinetics.

Age-dependent changes in ileal Cyp3a expression and protein levels in young, adult, and old mice. ( A ) Ileal Cyp3a mRNA expression normalized to Gapdh. ( B ) CYP3A protein levels normalized to GAPDH. ( C ) Representative Western blot images showing CYP3A and GAPDH protein expression in liver samples from each age group. Data are presented as mean ± SD ( n = 5 per group)
sections.discussion:
Our data demonstrate that ageing reshapes everolimus pharmacokinetics in male C57BL/6J mice in two distinct stages. From youth to adulthood, systemic exposure falls precipitously: C max and AUC are highest in young mice, intermediate in adults and lowest in olds, while apparent oral clearance increases three-fold and Vd/F more than doubles. Concomitantly, hepatic exposure reaches its nadir in adults, producing a U-shaped liver profile that rebounds in old animals. Mechanistic profiling identifies intestinal P-gp as the major age-sensitive barrier. Total ileal P-gp protein rises roughly four-fold in adults and remains high in olds, whereas intestinal Cyp3a expression is largely unchanged. It should be noted that the ‘old’ group in this study corresponds to a late middle-aged stage rather than advanced senescence, and therefore reflects early aging–associated pharmacokinetic alterations rather than end-of-life physiology.

We showed that ageing reshapes everolimus disposition in male C57BL/6J mice in a tissue-specific manner. Systemic exposure declined with increasing age: both C max and AUC were highest in young, intermediate in adult and lowest in old mice, while apparent oral clearance tripled and the apparent volume of distribution more than doubled from the youngest to the oldest group. Despite this systemic reduction, hepatic exposure displayed a U-shaped pattern, reaching its minimum in adult mice and rising again in old animals, suggesting age-dependent redistribution into liver tissue. Mechanistic profiling pointed to intestinal P-gp as the principal age-sensitive barrier. Total ileal P-gp protein increased approximately four-fold in adult mice and remained elevated in the old group, whereas intestinal CYP3A expression was largely unchanged. The inverse correlation between individual ileal P-gp levels and plasma AUC (ρ ≈ − 0.8) supports its dominant role in limiting oral absorption. In liver, Abcb1b rose with age but total P-gp protein fell, and CYP3A protein stayed relatively constant despite declining transcript levels, indicating post-transcriptional regulation and a lesser hepatic contribution to the systemic age effect. Overall, the data show that age-related up-regulation of intestinal P-gp, coupled with changes in tissue distribution, drives the reduced systemic exposure and the divergent hepatic accumulation of everolimus observed across the lifespan.

Our study is the first to demonstrate a clear chronological decline in systemic everolimus exposure: C max and AUC fell by roughly one-half from 9-week to 56-week males, while CL/F tripled and Vd/F more than doubled. Comparable rodent studies rarely stratify animals by age, with most experiments conducted in young adult mice (typically 6–20 weeks old) [ 25 ], regardless of the disease model, which leaves a notable pre-clinical gap in understanding age-related pharmacokinetic variability [ 26 ]. In humans, however, population pharmacokinetic (PK) analyses in large transplant and oncology cohorts (16–70 years) often fail to retain age as an independent covariate once factors such as body size, hematocrit, genotype, and drug–drug interactions are accounted for [ 27 , 28 ]. Older adults frequently have higher steady-state trough concentrations than younger adults for the same drug dose, largely due to age-related changes in drug metabolism and elimination. Older kidney transplant recipients had over 50% higher normalized calcineurin inhibitor troughs than younger adults, despite receiving lower doses [ 29 ]. The most consistent age-related pharmacokinetic effect in humans is the increased weight-normalized drug clearance in infants and young children, which justifies higher mg/m² dosing in this group [ 30 – 32 ]. In contrast, the pronounced age-related effects seen in rodent models do not directly translate to adult humans, most rodent studies use young animals, limiting relevance to human aging [ 25 , 26 ]. For clinical relevance, human studies rely on physiological markers rather than age alone, highlighting the need for careful interpretation and improved alignment of animal models with human aging.

In both rats and mice, age-related changes in P-glycoprotein (P-gp; Abcb1a/Abcb1b ) expression are tissue-specific and influenced by physiological or pathological status. In Fischer-344 rats, hepatic P-gp expression and transport function increase with age, suggesting an enhanced capacity for biliary drug efflux in older animals, whereas intestinal P-gp levels in the duodenum, ileum, and colon remain largely unchanged across the lifespan [ 33 ]. In disease states, such as streptozotocin-induced diabetes, these patterns are altered: hepatic Abcb1a mRNA rises in early diabetes but declines in later stages, Abcb1b mRNA is consistently reduced, and intestinal mucosa shows down-regulation of both isoforms with concomitant reductions in protein and activity [ 34 ]. In mice, direct age-stratified hepatic P-gp data are limited, and existing reports often derive from metabolic disease models rather than healthy ageing cohorts. For example, in a monosodium glutamate-induced obese, hyperglycemic C57BL/6J model, P-gp expression in the upper small intestine (duodenum, jejunum) increases with age, whereas the ileum shows no significant change [ 35 ]. This regional up-regulation likely reflects combined effects of metabolic stress and age, rather than chronological ageing alone.

Age-related changes in CYP3A expression are markedly tissue-specific and more consistently documented in rats than in mice. In the rat liver, CYP3A activity and protein abundance—particularly of isoforms such as CYP3A1, CYP3A2, and CYP3A18—decline substantially with age, with reported reductions of approximately 50–70%, indicating a diminished hepatic drug-metabolizing capacity in older animals [ 36 , 37 ]. In contrast, intestinal CYP3A levels, including predominant isoforms CYP3A9, CYP3A18, and CYP3A62, remain relatively stable throughout the duodenum, ileum, and colon across the lifespan [ 36 , 38 ]. Segmental expression is uneven, with higher levels in the proximal small intestine and a progressive decrease toward the colon [ 39 ], and some isoforms (e.g., CYP3A9, CYP3A62) exhibit female-predominant expression, especially in the liver [ 37 , 38 ]. For mice, direct age-stratified CYP3A expression data in healthy cohorts are lacking, but indirect evidence suggests that age-related changes in gut microbiota can modulate hepatic Cyp3a11 and other isoforms via nuclear receptor pathways such as PXR and CAR [ 40 , 41 ]. Additionally, metabolic disease models have shown altered intestinal CYP3A expression; for example, obesity-associated changes can decrease colonic Cyp3a mRNA [ 42 ].

Absolute F for everolimus is approximately 16% in healthy adults, ~ 5% in mice, 14–26% in rats, and ~ 6% in cynomolgus monkeys [ 43 ]. In our study, F appears to decline further with age, inferred from falling AUC without a shorter half-life and coincident intestinal P-gp induction. Age can alter oral drug bioavailability (F) primarily through its effects on first-pass metabolism and organ function, with the magnitude and direction of change depending on drug properties and individual physiology. For high first-pass drugs such as propranolol, labetalol, verapamil, and midazolam, ageing is often associated with increased F due to reduced hepatic extraction resulting from declines in liver mass and hepatic blood flow [ 2 , 44 – 47 ]. Changes in cytochrome P450 activity—particularly CYP3A4—are variable: some studies report stability across adulthood, while others show modest declines after age 70, potentially further reducing metabolism and increasing F for susceptible drugs [ 44 , 48 – 50 ]. In contrast, low-extraction drugs such as sotalol and digoxin generally show no age-related change in F [ 44 – 46 ]. Overall, the greatest age-related effects on F occur for high first-pass drugs, and while elderly patients may require dose reductions to avoid toxicity, dosing in both older adults and young children should be individualized with careful monitoring. Aging is associated with reduced plasma albumin concentration and binding capacity, age-related alterations in hepatic sinusoidal permeability, increased hepatic lipid content, and diminished liver blood flow—physiological changes that collectively favor enhanced hepatic partitioning of lipophilic drugs despite declining systemic exposure [ 15 , 51 – 54 ].

In mice, the two P-glycoprotein isoforms Abcb1a and Abcb1b exhibit clear tissue-specific expression patterns that likely have distinct functional consequences for drug disposition. Abcb1b predominates in the liver, whereas Abcb1a is the major isoform in the ileum, where it mediates most intestinal P-gp efflux activity. This distribution is consistent across studies and is modulated by multiple physiological and pathological factors. For example, intestinal Abcb1a displays pronounced circadian rhythmicity, leading to time-of-day–dependent variations in oral drug absorption [ 55 ], while hepatic Abcb1b lacks strong rhythmicity but can be upregulated with age or in disease states such as diabetes [ 34 , 56 , 57 ]. Conversely, diabetic models show reduced intestinal Abcb1a and P-gp, indicating tissue-divergent regulation under pathological conditions. The observed divergence between mRNA and protein levels—especially pronounced in aged liver—indicates post-transcriptional regulation, potentially mediated by microRNAs or accelerated proteasomal degradation [ 58 – 61 ]. These findings align with our observation of age-related increases in hepatic Abcb1b mRNA alongside reduced P-gp protein, and the sustained elevation of intestinal Abcb1a protein from adulthood into old age.

Taken together, these findings support a two-phase age model of everolimus disposition. While the transition from youth to adulthood is dominated by increased intestinal P-gp–mediated restriction of absorption, the divergence observed in old age cannot be explained by intestinal efflux alone. Instead, aging-related hepatic microenvironmental changes—including reduced albumin, increased lipid content, and altered sinusoidal permeability—likely promote tissue partitioning and intrahepatic sequestration, explaining the rebound in hepatic AUC despite continued declines in plasma exposure [ 51 , 53 , 54 ].

In contrast to the pronounced age-related modulation of intestinal P-gp and hepatic Cyp3a observed in mice, human data suggest far greater stability of these pathways across adult life. Human studies indicate substantial interindividual variability in CYP3A4 and P-gp expression (up to 8–10-fold), but no consistent age-related decline across adulthood; only modest reductions (≈ 20%) have been reported in postmenopausal women, and any observed decreases in metabolic capacity with aging are more likely attributable to broader physiological changes rather than to direct loss of enzyme expression [ 62 , 63 ]. Accordingly, chronological age alone is not considered a reliable determinant of everolimus exposure in humans [ 64 , 65 ]. These differences underscore the importance of cautious species extrapolation and support therapeutic drug monitoring, rather than empirical age-based dose adjustment, in older patients.

A limitation of the present study is the exclusive use of male mice. Our previous chronopharmacokinetic studies have demonstrated clear sex-dependent differences in everolimus disposition, with males showing higher systemic and tissue exposure and greater dose-related toxicity than females [ 23 , 66 , 67 ]. These observations suggest that females may exhibit lower bioavailability and/or enhanced metabolic clearance, potentially modifying age-related pharmacokinetic patterns. Accordingly, males were selected to isolate age effects in a model with higher exposure sensitivity, rather than to assume sex-independence. Nevertheless, whether the age-associated mechanisms identified here extend to females remains to be determined and warrants future investigation.
sections.conclusion: Overall, our findings position intestinal P-gp induction as the dominant age-variable barrier for everolimus in mice, whereas human adults experience modest age effects driven more by hepatic perfusion and clearance than by absorption. This divergence underscores the need for cautious species extrapolation and supports therapeutic-drug monitoring rather than empirical age-based dose adjustment for everolimus and most oral tyrosine kinase inhibitors in adults. Future work should include intravenous micro-dose studies, activity assays, and broader tissue distribution profiling in aged animals and very old patients to determine whether altered tissue sequestration poses a latent toxicity risk.
